stance_basis: letter and attached memo advocate for state/local flexibility, open-until-closed policy, and Wyoming-specific administration rather than blanket national rules
summary: The Wyoming Recreation Commission, through a letter from Director Paul H. Westedt and an attached memo from Chief of Planning Peter J. McNiff, expressed conditional support for ORV regulation while strongly urging that rules be flexible enough for state and local administration. They argued that Wyoming does not have the same ORV problems as heavily populated areas and that a 'closed until open' policy would create problems where none currently exist. Their detailed page-by-page comments on the draft EIS consistently pushed for an 'open until closed' philosophy and recognition of Wyoming's unique land-use situation.
complaint_summary: The extracted page-by-page comments from the Wyoming Recreation Commission's attachment raise specific objections to draft EIS language implying a 'closed until open' policy, unrealistic age requirements, inadequate mention of occupational/mineral-exploration ORV uses, and overly broad statements about environmental degradation that do not reflect Wyoming's situation.

statement.text:
Response #10, from Wyoming Recreation Commission,
Attachment to letter of 6/30/72 from Paul H. Westedt, and memorandum of 6/29/72, from Peter J. McNiff, to Paul H. Westedt.
Extracted below are comments made by above of draft ORV environmental statement (INT DES 72-62):
Comments:
Re: paragraph 1, on page 1 of EIS: "Implies an open until closed policy."
Re: paragraph 2, page 1 of EIS: Designation process "should not be used to close all and open only specific areas."
Re: Item 1, last paragraph of page 2 of EIS: "This coordination apparaently is not being done at this point; i.e. Governor's RCACT meeting, and if its not done now how can we expect the end product to be a coordinated effort.?
Re: Item 2, 4th paragraph, page 3 of EIS: "Implies an open until closed policy."
Re: Item iii, page 4 of EIS: "Implies a closed until open policy. The different type ORVs must be treated specifically. Snowmobiles cannot use the same area as dunebuggies, hence a lot of area is needed."
Re: Item b(i), page 5 of EIS: "Age requirement and 1 to 1 relationship is unrealistic and serves no purpose in Wyoming."
Re: Item iii, rage 5 of EIS: "Should add unless under a valid permit for a competitive event.
Re: Paragraph 3, page 6 of EIS: Re bonding "should be calrified so this cannot become a tool of arbitrary restrictive administration."
Re: First paragraph, page 12 of EIS: "Should be some mention of the 'working ORVs' mineral exploration, etc."
Re: Last sentence, page 13 of EIS: "This idea of identifying problem areas should be strengthened."
Re: Second paragraph, page 18 of EIS: "Again, needs some mention of work uses of ORVs."
Re: First paragraph, page 20 of EIS: "Again, this is implying the all closed until opened philosophy. Not the best way for Wyo. Concentration would create problems we don't have now."
<u>*</u> •

Continuation of extracted comments from Response #10, Wyoming Recreation Commission, re draft ORV environmental statement:
Re: Second paragraph, page 21 of EIS: "Wyo. has very successfully used the multiple use philosophy and to change from this into an all closed except where specifically open is asking for severe administrative problems."
Re: Page 22 of EIS: "Great - indicates an open until closed policy."
Re: First paragraph, page 24 of EIS: "This is not necessarily true in Wyo. This assumes that already a total capacity has been reached in valid areas of use. Should be reworded."
Re: First paragraph, page 25 of EIS: "To not only be sure that option to close is checked but the option for seasonal closures, etc. or reopening is kept open."
Re" Second paragraph, page 25 of EIS: "In Wyo. this must mean open until closed; a specific reason."
Re: Item VIII.A, page 26 of EIS: "Not the case in Wyo. The Forest Service stated at the REACT meeting that they are doing fine and plan some administration in the future." Add to last sentence of page 26:
"where such degradation is now taking place and the potential of new degration if use pressure in other areas reaches the critical point."
Re: Page 27 of EIS: "It should be mentioned that the involved agencies do have the power now to close areas and possibly the use of this power might solve the problem; i.e., as the Forest Service plans to do." Add to last sentence of page 27 of EIS: "where public use pressures have reached the critical point action must be taken."
Re: First paragraph, page 28 of EIS: Include "occupational use" of public lands.
Re: First paragraph, page 29 of EIS: "Should also be something here about established mineral exploration laws and also the effect on grazing permits, etc., which depend on CRV use."
Re: Third paragraph, page 30 of EIS: Add: "Also, the Department would be opening areas that have already administratively been closed for the protection of the area."
Re: First paragraph, page 31 of EIS: "Too broad a statement; i.e., Yellowstone and Grand Teton have a great deal of snowmobile use and it's working out fine."

Continuation of extracted comments from Response #10, Wyoming Recreation Commission, re draft ORV environmental statement:
Re: Next to last paragraph of page 31 of EIS: "We feel that both the ORV users and the objectors would rather have the rules and regulations do a fair and adequate job and to do this in Wyo. they must fit our special situation (not as we understand from local BLM representatives as an all closed except what is specifically open policy established by their Washington Office. In many cases the rules and regulations must be different to fit the situation. Wyo. cannot afford to be administrered by a policy established to administer lands in California or Minnesota."

statement.closing_anchor: Wyo. cannot afford to be administrered by a policy established to administer lands in California or Minnesota."

summary_quote: The first recommendation we would like to make in connection with the above mentioned draft is that procedures be established to insure that any rules and regulations adopted in connection with this subject have sufficient built-in flexibility to allow for administration on the state and local level, thus enabling their adjustment to the existing situations.
